## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- **Describe** the multilayer-perceptron architecture (input to hidden to output) and **state**
  what universal approximation does and does not promise. *(Understand)*

## Why This Matters

L14 ended on a cliffhanger. We proved a two-layer network *can* solve XOR — but only because we
played god and set every weight by hand. That does not scale: a real network has thousands to
billions of weights and no human to place them. This lesson removes the training wheels. It
introduces the **multilayer perceptron (MLP)** as the general architecture, states the theorem
that makes MLPs worth using (**universal approximation**), and then *learns* the weights from data
with **PyTorch**, the course's deep-learning framework.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
L14 was sculpting a statue by placing every grain of clay by hand. L15 is pouring the clay into a
mold and letting **gradient descent** settle it into shape. We still watch every step of the pour
— forward, loss, backward, step — we just no longer place each grain ourselves.
:::

## The MLP Architecture

A **multilayer perceptron** stacks the neurons of L14 into layers:

- an **input layer** (one value per feature),
- one or more **hidden layers** of neurons (each a dense layer + a nonlinear activation),
- an **output layer** whose shape is chosen by the task.

Signal flows one way, input to output — a **feedforward** network. A net with a *deep* stack of
hidden layers is a **deep neural network (DNN)**, and studying those is what "deep learning" means.
For one hidden layer, the whole model is two of L14's layer equations chained:

$$
\mathbf{h} = \phi(\mathbf{W}_1\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_1), \qquad
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{W}_2\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{b}_2 .
$$

The **output layer** is picked to match the problem: **K logits** (then softmax) for K-class
classification, or **one linear unit** for regression. The hidden layers are where the network
builds its own useful features — exactly the "act on what the previous layer computed" idea from
L14.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  subgraph IN["input layer"]
    X1(("x1")); X2(("x2"))
  end
  subgraph H["hidden layer (ReLU)"]
    H1(("h1")); H2(("h2")); H3(("h3"))
  end
  subgraph OUT["output layer"]
    O1(("logit 1")); O2(("logit 2"))
  end
  X1 --> H1 & H2 & H3
  X2 --> H1 & H2 & H3
  H1 --> O1 & O2
  H2 --> O1 & O2
  H3 --> O1 & O2
```

## Universal Approximation

Why expect a pile of neurons to fit anything useful? Because of a remarkable result: a network
with **one hidden layer**, given **enough units**, can approximate **any continuous function** to
arbitrary accuracy. MLPs are universal shape-fitters. In the lab you watch this directly — a
one-hidden-layer net fits a wiggly curve worse with one unit (MSE 0.465) and almost perfectly with
sixteen (MSE 0.0002).

::: {.callout-important title="What universal approximation does NOT promise"}
It is an **existence** result. It says a good fit *exists* — not how **many** units you need, not
that **gradient descent will find** it, and not that one ultra-wide layer is the *efficient* shape
(stacking several hidden layers — going **deep** — usually reaches the same accuracy with far fewer
units). "Can approximate anything" is a reason MLPs are worth training, not a promise that training
is easy.
:::

## Meet PyTorch

We learn the weights with **PyTorch** (the course's deep-learning framework; classic ML stayed on
scikit-learn). Two pieces are enough to start:

- A **tensor** is PyTorch's n-dimensional array — think a NumPy array that can also track the
  gradients needed for training.
- A **model** is built by stacking layers with `nn.Sequential`. Our lab classifier is literally

  ```python
  model = nn.Sequential(
      nn.Linear(2, 16),   # dense layer: 2 inputs -> 16 hidden units
      nn.ReLU(),          # nonlinear activation
      nn.Linear(16, 2),   # -> 2 logits (one per class)
  )
  ```

  That is the architecture diagram above, in code. The model is just a function: feed it inputs,
  it returns logits.

## The Training Loop

Unlike scikit-learn's one-line `.fit()`, in PyTorch we write the loop ourselves — because *seeing*
it is the whole point of this unit. Each pass over the data (an **epoch**) repeats four steps:

```python
optimizer.zero_grad()           # clear last step's gradients (they accumulate)
logits = model(x)               # 1. forward  — predict
loss   = loss_fn(logits, y)     # 2. loss     — measure the error
loss.backward()                 # 3. backward — compute every gradient
optimizer.step()                # 4. step     — nudge the weights downhill
```

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  F["forward<br/>logits = model(x)"] --> L["loss<br/>loss_fn(logits, y)"]
  L --> B["backward()<br/>autograd -> gradients"]
  B --> S["optimizer.step()<br/>gradient descent"]
  S -->|next epoch| F
```

Three of the four steps are old friends: the **forward** pass is just prediction, the **loss** is
the error (L04's log loss, here `CrossEntropyLoss`), and the **step** is one move of **gradient
descent** (L03). The new line is `loss.backward()`: it computes how every weight should change to
reduce the loss — all 82 of them at once, automatically. We treat **`backward()` as a black box**
in this lesson; opening it is exactly what L16 (Backpropagation & Autodiff) is for.

::: {.callout-note title="Logits, not probabilities"}
`nn.CrossEntropyLoss` expects **raw logits** — it applies the (log-)softmax internally. So the
model's last layer outputs logits with **no** softmax attached; adding one would double-count and
train worse. To read **probabilities** at inference time, apply `softmax` to the logits *then*,
outside the loss.
:::

## Common Pitfalls

- **Adding a `softmax` before `CrossEntropyLoss`.** The loss already does it; a second softmax
  hurts. Emit logits; apply softmax only at inference to read probabilities.
- **Forgetting `optimizer.zero_grad()`.** Gradients **accumulate** across steps in PyTorch; skip
  the clear and each step adds to the last, corrupting training.
- **Not standardizing inputs.** Like every distance/gradient-based method (L08, L10), an MLP trains
  far better on standardized features; fit the scaler on the training set only.
- **Reading universal approximation as "easy".** "Can approximate anything" is existence, not a
  recipe — you still choose width/depth and rely on gradient descent to find the fit.
- **No nonlinearity = no depth.** A stack of `nn.Linear` with no activations collapses to one
  linear layer (L14). The `nn.ReLU()` between layers is mandatory.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Why write the loop instead of calling `.fit()`?"** — Because the forward / loss / `backward()` /
step cycle *is* the subject of this unit. scikit-learn hides it; PyTorch shows it, which is what
lets the next lessons open up backprop (L16) and tune the optimizer and regularization (L17). In
production you often use higher-level helpers, but you must understand the loop they wrap.

**"Why logits instead of probabilities?"** — Numerical stability and correctness: `CrossEntropyLoss`
combines log-softmax and the negative-log-likelihood in one numerically safe step. Emitting a
softmax yourself and then taking its log is worse-behaved. Read probabilities with `softmax` only
when you actually need them, at inference.

**"How many layers and units should I use?"** — There is no formula. More capacity can fit more but
risks overfitting (L09); universal approximation guarantees a fit *exists*, not that a given size
finds it. Start small, add capacity if you underfit, regularize if you overfit — the systematic
tools for deep nets are L17.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---|---|
| MLP | input layer to one+ hidden dense layers (nonlinear) to an output layer |
| Output layer | K logits + softmax for classification; one linear unit for regression |
| Deep network (DNN) | an MLP with a deep stack of hidden layers |
| Universal approximation | one hidden layer, enough units, approximates any continuous function (existence, not a recipe) |
| PyTorch model | `nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(...), nn.ReLU(), ...)` — a function from inputs to logits |
| Training loop | `zero_grad` -> forward -> loss -> `backward()` -> `step`, each epoch |
| `loss.backward()` | autograd computes every gradient (the black box; mechanism is L16) |
| Logits + `CrossEntropyLoss` | emit raw logits; the loss applies softmax — never add your own |

  one hidden layer suffices to approximate any continuous function.
